sections.origins_and_history: Waacking originated in Los Angeles during the early 1970s inside LGBTQ+ nightclubs, created primarily by African American and Latino dancers. It began as punking, a name derived from a derogatory slur aimed at gay men, which performers inverted into an expressive, narrative dance style. Dancers moved to underground and imported disco music that DJs sped up to produce an intense, energetic atmosphere. The specific technique of driving the arms over the head in rhythm became known as 'whack'. Heterosexual dancers who encountered the style renamed it whacking to distance themselves from anti-gay terminology, after which gay culture reclaimed and reshaped the term into 'waacking', formalized when Soul Train dancer and singer-songwriter Jeffrey Daniel added the 'g'. During the 1980s and 1990s, the AIDS crisis killed most of the style's iconic pioneers, driving the dance close to extinction until Brian 'Footwork' Green began teaching it in 2003 to ensure its transmission.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The style is executed through rapid, rotational arm sweeps, explosive rhythmic strikes, and theatrical poses coordinated with music. Dancers whip their forearms and wrists around and behind the head and across the shoulder line, isolating sharp gestures while maintaining rhythmic syncopation. A key technical element is posing, in which dancers freeze into glamorous, heightened diva stances inspired by Hollywood movie figures. The dance prioritizes facial expression, sensuality, and dramatic storytelling, allowing the performer to embody distinct attitudes and narrative moods. Footwork in the sources incorporates elements derived from jazz, gymnastics, martial arts, and hip-hop influences, though the central visual hallmark remains overhead arm isolations danced to fast tempos.
sections.music_and_instruments: Waacking was founded on 1970s disco and funk, specifically underground and imported disco records that were often sped up on club turntables to increase dance floor energy. Over subsequent decades, the dance adapted to 1980s post-disco, electro sounds, and modern music varieties, though disco remains its historical and primary sonic foundation. The music is characterized by steady four-on-the-floor percussion, driving basslines, orchestral sweeps, and brass hits that provide sharp rhythmic accents for explosive arm strikes and sudden poses.
sections.costume_and_setting: Originally performed in dimly lit LGBTQ+ nightclubs of 1970s Los Angeles, waacking was framed by social freedom and theatrical display. Dancers drew visual and sartorial inspiration from classic Hollywood screen stars such as Marlene Dietrich, Lauren Bacall, and James Dean, adopting vintage diva attitudes, tailored silhouettes, and stylized garments. In modern practice, waacking appears in international dance battles, television studios, university theatre departments, music videos, and competitive ice rinks, where performers continue to wear expressive, high-fashion, and dramatic attire.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: In its original gay club context, punking and waacking served as an outlet of creative liberation, sensual expression, and self-definition for marginalized queer, Black, and Latino dancers facing social hostility. The dance provided a theatrical space to emulate glamorous Hollywood divas and enact personal stories through heightened physicality. Today, waacking is performed at competitive street dance battles, theatre showcases, university dance curricula, pop concerts, and global sports ceremonies, retaining its ethos of unapologetic self-expression and dramatic presence.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical and contemporary figures include Jeffrey Daniel, who added the 'g' to the name; Tyrone Proctor (1953–2020), a pioneering Los Angeles creator and Soul Train dancer; Brian 'Footwork' Green, who initiated the 2003 global revival through workshops; Kumari Suraj, who choreographed a milestone 2011 routine on So You Think You Can Dance; and French waacker Josépha Madoki, who danced in the 2018 'Apeshit' music video by Beyoncé and Jay-Z. Other notable practitioners named in sources include Bruno Marignan, Sandrine Sainte Croix, Lil Kiss, Princess Lockeroo, Mariana Benenge, Mounia Nassangar, Habibitch, Boubou, choreographer Axelle Munezero, and Olympic champions Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron.
sections.regional_variants: Waacking originated in Los Angeles, California, developing alongside New York City's parallel ballroom voguing culture on the East Coast of the United States. While early waacking was centered in southern California venues and national broadcast sets like Soul Train, contemporary regional hubs have expanded globally. France has emerged as a significant center through artists like Josépha Madoki, Princess Lockeroo, and choreographers who adapted the style for theater and international competition.
sections.lineage: Waacking evolved directly out of punking in 1970s Los Angeles gay clubs, absorbing stylistic and physical principles from jazz dance, gymnastics, martial arts, and Hollywood screen performance. It developed alongside locking within the Los Angeles street dance ecosystem and runs historically parallel to East Coast voguing. In modern lineages, waacking has exchanged vocabulary with hip-hop dance and entered university dance departments as well as commercial performance repertoires.

claims.text: Waacking originated from punking, a dance created in the gay clubs of Los Angeles during the 1970s disco era.
The movement was characterized by moving the arms rhythmically over the head.
Jeffrey Daniel modified the name from waackin to waacking.
Dancers took stylistic inspiration from classic Hollywood screen stars.
The dance style was developed by the LGBTQ+ community, especially African American and Latino dancers.
The AIDS crisis in the 1980s and 1990s killed most iconic dancers, leading waacking to almost disappear.
Brian Green began teaching waacking in 2003 to address the lack of transmission.
Gabriella Papadakis and Guillaume Cizeron won gold at the 2022 Winter Olympics with a program influenced by waacking.

sections.origins_and_history: Ballet de cour developed in late 16th-century France out of medieval processions, mummeries, and Italian Renaissance court festivals. Catherine de' Medici championed these entertainments following her 1533 marriage to Henri II, bringing Italian staging concepts to Paris. The Académie de Poésie et de Musique, established in 1570 by Jean-Antoine de Baif and Thibault de Courville, provided the philosophical ambition to harmonize dance, verse, and music. Key early spectacles included the Ballet des Polonais in 1573 and the Ballet Comique de la Reine in 1581, directed by Balthasar de Beaujoyeulx. Production expanded under Louis XIII and reached its political apex under Louis XIV and Cardinal Mazarin, with Isaac de Benserade authoring texts. The genre faded after Louis XIV withdrew from dancing in 1670.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performances occurred in great halls with the audience stacked on three surrounding tiers, making overhead geometric floor designs central to the choreography. Dancers executed intricate patterns, swerves, sinuosities, interlacings, confrontations, and retreats. The work unfolded in structured entrées where performers danced by turn, culminating in the Grand Ballet with the entire cast, followed by an open social ball where spectators joined the performers. Specific individual foot mechanics, counts, and step names for the earliest period are not described in sources beyond Beaujoyeulx's use of measure and geometry, Thoinot Arbeau's 1589 foundations, and Pierre Beauchamp's subsequent codification of the five positions.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical framework encompassed vocal and instrumental pieces, featuring an opening overture with recitation followed by vocal airs, choruses, and instrumental dances accompanying each entrée. Violins and court instrumental ensembles accompanied the dancers. Central composers across the era included Pierre Guédron, Antoine Boësset, Étienne Moulinié, Michael Praetorius, and Jean-Baptiste Lully, whose collaborations with Pierre Beauchamp elevated ballet music to an equal partner with movement.
sections.costume_and_setting: Spectacles were staged in large palace halls, such as the Tuileries Palace and the Louvre, before the advent of the proscenium stage. Decor was lavish, featuring elaborate scenic machinery such as chariot-floats, palaces, gardens, townscapes, and three-tiered fountains. Costumes were ornate aristocratic dress, later evolving toward lighter apparel and flexible footwear by the late 17th century.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Ballets de cour marked royal weddings, state receptions of foreign ambassadors, and celebrations of political triumphs. As a secular ceremony designed to exalt the State and project royal power, it communicated harmony, virtue, and monarchical dominance, often using classical allegory to symbolize national reconciliation after religious civil strife.
sections.notable_figures: Key historic figures include Queen Catherine de' Medici; choreographer and master of revels Balthasar de Beaujoyeulx (Baldassarino de Belgioioso); poet Isaac de Benserade; Académie founders Jean-Antoine de Baif and Thibault de Courville; monarchs Henri III, Louis XIII, and Louis XIV; composer Jean-Baptiste Lully; and ballet superintendent Pierre Beauchamp.
sections.regional_variants: Originating in the French royal court in Paris and its royal residences (such as the Tuileries, the Louvre, and Chantilly), the form rapidly spread to courts across Europe, contrasting with Italian opera which concentrated more heavily on singing than physical choreography.
sections.lineage: Evolved from medieval mummeries and Italian Renaissance court festivals into French court ballet; later transformed into comédie-ballet and opéra-ballet, directly providing the technical and organizational foundation for codified classical ballet.

claims.text: Ballet de cour is the term given to ballets performed at royal courts during the 16th and 17th centuries.
The early ballet de cour was a secular event whose primary political objective was the exaltation of the state.
Early choreographies were designed as geometric figures meant to be observed from above by audiences seated on three sides.
In 1573, Catherine de' Medici commissioned the Ballet des Polonais, performed by sixteen noblewomen representing the sixteen provinces of France.
The five-hour Ballet Comique de la Reine was staged in 1581 to celebrate the wedding of Marguerite of Lorraine and the Duc de Joyeuse.
The 17th-century court ballet was structured with an overture, thematic entrées, and a final Grand Ballet.
When Louis XIV stopped dancing in court productions in 1670, it dealt a fatal blow to ballet de cour and gave rise to comédie-ballet and opéra-ballet.

episode_brief.logline: From the Tuileries to Versailles, French monarchs used lavish five-hour geometric spectacles to turn dancing courtiers into instruments of state power.

sections.origins_and_history: The farruca developed as a flamenco style in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The word relates to 'farruco', an Andalusian term applied to immigrants from Galicia or Asturias, as well as a familiar nickname for Francisco. While lyric references to Galician bagpipes and landscape led many to claim a northern origin, musicologists note this has not been scientifically proven. Instead, it was adapted into flamenco (aflamencado) within theatrical venues, zarzuela, and cafés cantantes like Café Madrid and Café del Recreo in Cádiz. In 1907, composer José Serrano included a farruca in his sainete Alma de Dios. In 1908, dancer Faíco and guitarist Ramón Montoya consolidated the canonical dance and guitar forms.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The farruca is danced as a dramatic solo characterized by upright posture, sharp footwork (zapateado), held poses, sudden pauses, turns, and abrupt directional changes. Performed within an eight-beat compás consisting of two 4/4 bars with accents on 1, 3, 5, and 7, it begins at a moderate, articulated tempo. Choreographies proceed from an entrance (salida) into marked compás, llamadas, remates, and extended escobillas. Dancers use double-time footwork, contratiempos, and level changes, driving through an acceleration (subida) toward a final llamada or cierre, sometimes finishing with the rhythm of a tanguillo or rumba.
sections.music_and_instruments: Farruca music is grounded in binary or quadruple meter (two measures of 4/4) with strong accents on counts 1, 3, 5, and 7. The primary accompanying instrument is the flamenco guitar, traditionally played in A minor or E minor, characterized by alternation between E7 and A minor, rasgueados, falsetas, and golpes. While often performed as an instrumental piece without cante, traditional verses feature four octosyllabic lines with assonant rhyme, descending contours on final vowels, and vocables such as 'tran tran tran treiro'.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance emerged within theatrical spaces, varieté, and cafés cantantes before transitioning to concert halls and ballet stages. Performers wear attire that accentuates vertical line and sharp posture, traditionally consisting of high-waisted trousers, fitted waistcoats, and flamenco boots suitable for virtuosic footwork. Historical descriptions document the use of a cape during early male stage performances. Early female dancers frequently performed the dance dressed in male clothing.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Farruca carries an austere, dramatic, and sombre character linked symbolically to valor and restraint. Unlike communal festive palos, it is primarily a theatrical and concert performance form. Its dramatic gravity was spotlighted in major theatrical works, including Manuel de Falla's 1919 ballet El sombrero de tres picos (as the Miller's Dance / Danse du meunier) choreographed by Léonide Massine, and Carlos Saura's film Carmen featuring Antonio Gades.
sections.notable_figures: Dancer Faíco (Francisco Mendoza Ríos) and guitarist Ramón Montoya are recognized as the primary architects of the modern dance and guitar structure. Dancers El Gato, Antonio de Bilbao, Manolito la Rosa, El Batato, Antonio Gades, El Güito, Mario Maya, and Manolete further codified its stage aesthetic. Groundbreaking women dancers who reshaped the form include Rafaela Valverde 'La Tanguera', Carmen Amaya, and Sara Baras. Prominent guitar interpreters include Sabicas, Carlos Montoya, Paco Peña, Manolo Sanlúcar, and Paco de Lucía.
sections.regional_variants: Technique not described in sources beyond local café cantante traditions and theatrical adaptations.
sections.lineage: Farruca belongs to the aflamencado group of non-Andalusian folkloric forms along with the garrotín. It shares a binary 4/4 compás with tangos and tientos, the tempo feel of tanguillos, and occasionally adopts elements of rumba or tanguillo during its closing stretta.

sections.origins_and_history: Yove male mome, also known as Povela e Yova, originates from the traditional dance Jove from the Shopluk region of Bulgaria. In 1966, US folk dance instructor Dennis Boxell introduced its choreography outside of Bulgaria at an event in Stockton, California. Following this introduction, the dance became widely popular among international folk dancers across the globe.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed as a fast, complicated line dance arranged in a curved line or open circle. Dancers link together by holding their neighbours by the belt, or by the hands if belts are not worn. Structurally, one common version consists of seven patterns containing four bars each. Dancers follow an 18/16 meter divided into alternating sub-bars of 7/16 and 11/16, counted as 3-2-2 and 2-2-3-2-2, or slow-quick-quick, quick-quick-slow-quick-quick.
sections.music_and_instruments: Musical renditions of Yove male mome are played in an 18/16 compound meter (7+11/16), incorporating alternating sub-bars of common chetvorno (7/16) and kopanitsa (11/16) rhythms. The melody and accompaniment often feature the traditional Bulgarian gaida (bagpipe). The accompanying lyrics belong to the folk song Povela e Yova, telling the story of Yova leading two horses to water.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance takes place in social and recreational settings in a curved line or open circle. In traditional contexts, dancers wear belts, which are essential for the traditional grip where each dancer holds their neighbours by the belt; handholds are used when belts are absent.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally danced to communal folk songs in the Shopluk region, the dance is tied to the lyrical narrative of Yova watering horses—giving clear water to her beloved's horse and murky water to her brother's horse. Today, it is widely performed at folk dance clubs, workshops, and recreational Balkan dance gatherings worldwide.
sections.notable_figures: US folk dance instructor Dennis Boxell played a pivotal role in disseminating the dance by introducing its choreography outside Bulgaria in Stockton, California, in 1966. Folklorist Manol Todorov documented the song's lyrics in his 1976 work Balgarska narodna muzika, and Bulgarian singer Hristina Boteva is known for performing the song.
sections.regional_variants: The dance originates from the Shopluk region of Bulgaria under the traditional name Jove. Beyond regional village variants, it is known under variant names such as Jove male mome, Jove malaj mome, and Povela e Yova.
sections.lineage: Yove male mome derives directly from the regional Shopluk dance Jove. Its rhythmic structure embeds the metrics of both chetvorno (7/16) and kopanitsa (11/16), representing a hybrid compound form within the broader family of Bulgarian horo line dances.

basic_steps: Grasp neighbouring dancers firmly by the belt or link hands if belts are not available.
Stand in an open circle or curved line facing slightly along the line of direction.
Execute the 7/16 sub-bar with a slow step on count 1 (three pulses) followed by two quick steps on counts 2 and 3 (two pulses each).
Execute the 11/16 sub-bar with two quick steps on counts 1 and 2 (two pulses each), one slow step on count 3 (three pulses), and two quick steps on counts 4 and 5 (two pulses each).
Progress through the seven choreographic patterns of four bars each while maintaining the line curvature.

sections.origins_and_history: Tribal Fusion emerged from the California belly dance lineage tracing back to Jamila Salimpour, who founded the troupe Bal Anat in the late 1960s to present theatrical Middle Eastern and North African styles at California Renaissance fairs. Jamila taught Masha Archer of the San Francisco Classic Dance Troupe, who in turn taught Carolena Nericcio, the founder of FatChanceBellyDance and pioneer of American Tribal Style (ATS). In the late 1990s, Jill Parker—a student of Nericcio—founded Ultra Gypsy, considered the first tribal fusion dance company, scaling down the traditional costume and choreographing to contemporary DJ-mixed tracks. Simultaneously, Heather Stants introduced minimalist aesthetics and modern dance concepts through Urban Tribal Dance Company in 1999, while Rachel Brice codified the name 'Tribal Fusion' during email correspondence with Nericcio and popularized the movement globally.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Unlike the strictly group-led, cue-based structured improvisation of FatChanceBellyDance, Tribal Fusion is predominantly choreographed and can be performed as a solo, duet, or group piece. Dancers maintain an upright lifted posture while executing hyper-articulated isolations, including popping contractions, belly rolls, serpentine arm paths, and hip locks. Dancers integrate technique derived from Suhaila Salimpour, hip hop popping, flamenco arm carriage, and Indian classical forms like Kathak and Odissi. Movement shifts rapidly between slow, fluid muscular sinuosity and explosive percussive accents.
sections.music_and_instruments: Tribal Fusion evolved alongside late-1990s and early-2000s electronica, trip-hop, and world fusion. Producers and DJs merged traditional Middle Eastern acoustic instruments—such as darbuka, riqq, and oud—with synthesized beats, deep bass lines, and breakbeats. Key figures shaping the sound include Cheb i Sabbah, Bassnectar, Amon Tobin, Squarepusher, Solace (Jeremiah Soto), Pete List, and Beats Antique, creating what became known as the electronica Oriental genre.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costuming varies between rich maximalism and sleek modern minimalism. The adorned aesthetic, popularized by Mardi Love and The Indigo, features layered skirts, Tulle bi telli fabrics, antique tribal jewelry, Afghan guls, Indian shisha mirrors, and Rajasthani cowrie shells braided into the hair with dyed yarn. Tattoos, body piercings, and dramatic stage makeup are common. Conversely, the urban tribal branch championed by Heather Stants adopts minimalist, contemporary dance-inspired attire. Settings range from traditional haflas and belly dance festivals to theatrical stages and music festivals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Tribal Fusion is primarily a theatrical and performance art form rather than a social or ritual dance. It is performed on concert stages, community haflas, circus-theatre showcases, and alternative music events. Moving away from the commercial cabaret nightclub format, it emphasizes artistic self-expression, bodily mastery, strength, and female stage presence uncoupled from exoticized male-gaze entertainment.
sections.notable_figures: Seminal figures include Jill Parker ('mama of Tribal Fusion'), Heather Stants (founder of Urban Tribal Dance Company), Rachel Brice (foremost soloist and co-founder of The Indigo), Mardi Love (costume innovator and core member of The Indigo), Zoe Jakes (co-founder of Beats Antique), Suhaila Salimpour (whose isolation technique heavily influenced the movement), Ariellah Aflalo (Dark Fusion pioneer), and producer Miles Copeland.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include Urban Tribal, developed in San Diego with modern dance and street aesthetics; Dark Fusion, initiated by Ariellah Aflalo blending gothic elements; Vaudeville or Tribal Vintage, drawing from pre-WWII jazz, swing, and burlesque eras; and Improvisational Tribal Style (ITS), developed by Amy Sigil as an alternate group-improvisation framework.
sections.lineage: Traced through a direct teacher-student chain: Jamila Salimpour taught Masha Archer; Archer taught Carolena Nericcio (creator of ATS); Nericcio taught Jill Parker; Parker inspired Heather Stants and Mardi Love; technique was further shaped by Suhaila Salimpour; Rachel Brice consolidated these lines to form Tribal Fusion.

basic_steps: Lift ribcage and drop shoulders into an aligned, grounded stance with soft knees.
Execute an upper-torso chest slide side-to-side without moving the hips.
Roll the abdomen sequentially in an undulating belly roll, pulling inward from top to bottom.
Perform a sharp pelvic tuck and release isolation (lock or pop) on a percussive beat count.
Extend arms outward, creating continuous serpentine shoulder-to-wrist arm waves while maintaining torso stillness.
teaching.rhythm: Downtempo electronic 4/4 or syncopated world-fusion percussion; movement layers slow continuous undulations over sharp rhythmic locks.
teaching.formation: Solo performance, duet, or choreographed ensemble lines; does not require the lead-and-follow chorus formation of ATS.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners focus on muscular isolation of the ribcage, pelvic locks, and decoupling arm movements from torso shifts.

claims.text: Tribal Fusion was created by fusing American Tribal Style belly dance and American Cabaret belly dance.
Jill Parker's company Ultra Gypsy was the first Tribal Fusion dance company.
In 1999 Heather Stants founded Urban Tribal Dance Company in San Diego with a minimalist aesthetic.
Mardi Love popularized Rajasthani cowrie falls using hand-dyed yarn for Tribal Fusion hair adornments.
Tribal Fusion is choreographed and can be performed as a solo.
The lineage runs from Jamila Salimpour through Masha Archer, Carolena Nericcio, Jill Parker, Heather Stants, and Mardi Love to Rachel Brice.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Heavy electronic downbeats accented with syncopated Middle Eastern doumbek patterns (e.g., maqsum or baladi frameworks) and glitch/breakbeat subdivisions.
instruments: Acoustic brass and clarinet (in vaudeville styles)
music_profile.vocal_style: Predominantly instrumental, occasionally featuring ambient world vocal samples, dark vocalizations, or vintage jazz phrasing.
music_profile.musical_form: Contemporary electronic track structure with evolving ambient textures, heavy bass drops, and recurring melodic ostinatos.
music_profile.sound_description: A dense synthesis of subterranean sub-bass, digitized breakbeats, and acoustic Middle Eastern percussion, textured with swirling ambient synthesizer pads, melancholic string motifs, and occasional swing or jazz brass accents.

movement_profile.posture: Grounded lower body with soft knees, an elevated and wide ribcage, engaged core, flat lower back, and lengthened neck with relaxed shoulders.
movement_profile.footwork: Slow deliberate stepping, lunges, and controlled weight transfers coordinated with rhythmic counts; footwork remains subordinate to upper-body and pelvic isolations.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Sinuous snake arms undulating through shoulders, elbows, and wrists; stark geometric framing influenced by flamenco and popping; delicate Mudra-inspired hand placement.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Precise separation between thoracic and pelvic compartments; rolling abdominal undulations; sharp popping locks of the pelvis; figure-eight hip pathways.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Fluid stage floor patterns, direct audience address, diagonal transitions, and stationary solo pedestals.
movement_profile.partnering: Unpartnered solo or synchronized ensemble choreography; contact partnering is rare, though visual echoing and staged duets occur.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Intensely polyrhythmic: often moving the upper body in slow, half-time fluid pathways while hips or muscles execute rapid, on-beat pops and hits.

signature_moves.name: Snake Arms
signature_moves.description: Continuous, alternating wave-like undulation passing from the scapula through the shoulder, elbow, and wrist out to the fingertips.

signature_moves.name: Belly Roll
signature_moves.description: Sequential contraction and release of upper and lower abdominal muscles producing a fluid vertical rolling motion.

signature_moves.name: Ribcage Isolation Slide
signature_moves.description: Linear horizontal translation of the ribcage parallel to the floor without shifting the pelvis or hips.

signature_moves.name: Pelvic Pop/Lock
signature_moves.description: Crisp, instantaneous contraction of pelvic and gluteal muscles creating a distinct sudden accent.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Extensive level changes including deep floorwork, knee drops, and backbends; no aerial jumps or elevated leaps.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid moving the pelvis and ribcage simultaneously during single isolations; avoid collapsing the thoracic spine or hyperextending knees.

episode_brief.title_hook: Isolations in the Underground: How California Re-Engineered Belly Dance
episode_brief.logline: Tracing the evolution of belly dance from 1960s California counterculture to the bass-heavy stages of electronic music festivals via Jill Parker and Rachel Brice.

sections.origins_and_history: The robot dance evolved from early 20th-century mime acts that imitated mechanical figures. In the late 1960s, it transitioned into social dance in American funk and soul clubs, pioneered by Charles "Robot" Washington and "Robot Ann" who danced it socially to music. Michael Jackson popularized the dance globally in 1973 with televised performances of "Dancing Machine". The robot is related to but distinct from popping, sharing some movements but focusing on mechanical illusion rather than muscle pops.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers maintain a rigid, mechanical posture, moving limbs in segmented, stilted motions. Each movement begins and ends with a dimestop—an abrupt halt simulating a motor starting or stopping. The dance can be performed solo or socially, with or without music. Rhythmically, it aligns best with music featuring distinct, steady beats like electrofunk. Technique involves controlling muscle tension to create the illusion of robotic movement. Beginners start by practicing slow, isolated limb movements with clear stops.
sections.music_and_instruments: The robot is often danced to music with clear, steady beats such as electrofunk, which enhances the mechanical illusion. Music with a 'robot theme' is also common, even if not rhythmically ideal. The dance can be performed silently as mime or accompanied by beatboxing and mechanical sound effects. Instruments typical in electrofunk include synthesizers, drum machines, and bass guitar, producing a steady, electronic groove.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costuming is flexible; social dancers in the 1960s wore typical funk or soul club attire. Performance costumes may emphasize a mechanical or futuristic look with metallic colors or angular designs. The dance is performed in clubs, on television, and in street settings. No sacred or restricted costume conventions apply.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally part of theatrical mime and social dancing at funk and soul parties, the robot became a performance dance symbolizing mechanical and futuristic themes. It is performed socially, in competitions, on television, and in popular media. The dance is not sacred or restricted.
sections.notable_figures: Charles "Robot" Washington and "Robot Ann" pioneered social robot dancing to music. Michael Jackson popularized the robot globally with his 1973 Soul Train performance of "Dancing Machine". Mime artist Robert Shields influenced the style through mechanical mime acts.
sections.regional_variants: The robot originated in the United States and spread globally through media exposure. Variants exist within popping and street dance communities, sometimes blending with locking or liquid dancing styles.
sections.lineage: The robot descends from early 20th-century mime traditions and evolved through 1960s American funk social dance. It is closely related to popping and locking street dance styles but remains a distinct form focused on mechanical illusion.

basic_steps: Stand upright with a rigid posture.
Isolate one arm and move it slowly in a segmented motion.
Perform a dimestop by abruptly halting the arm movement.
Repeat with the other arm and legs, maintaining mechanical stiffness.
Combine limb movements with stops to simulate robot motors.
teaching.rhythm: Best danced to music with distinct, steady beats such as electrofunk.
teaching.formation: Typically solo or small groups; social couple dancing also practiced.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners focus on slow, isolated movements and clear stops; advanced dancers relax muscles subtly while maintaining illusion.

claims.text: The robot, also called mannequin or dancing machine, is a street dance style—often confused with popping—that suggests the stilted movements of a dancing robot or mannequin.
Roboting gained fame in the 1970s after Michael Jackson used the dance when he performed "Dancing Machine" with his brothers.
Movements of the robot are normally started and finished with a dimestop (a very abrupt stop), to give the impression of motors starting and stopping.
Charles "Robot" Washington and his partner "Robot Ann" were the first to socially couple dance the style to music at parties and clubs.
The Jackson 5 first performed "Dancing Machine" on Soul Train on November 3, 1973, where Michael Jackson performed a robot dance during the song's musical break.
All robot movements begin and end with a locking step, giving the impression of a motor starting or stopping.

sections.origins_and_history: Fisounis is a Greek dance originating from the region of Preveza in Epirus. sections.origins_and_history: Orteke originated in southwestern Kazakhstan and spread across Central Asian nomadic pastoral cultures, including regions of Uzbekistan. The name joins 'or' (a ditch, hole, or pit trap) with 'teke' (a buck or male mountain goat). Scholars and ethnographers argue that the practice originated in prehistory, potentially serving ancient shamans as a tool to distract spirits or act as a spirit vessel during therapeutic and healing rites. Although the craft holds ancient roots among Turkic tribes, wider distribution occurred during the nineteenth century. In the 1930s, the performance was presented at the Almaty Puppet Theatre, and in 1935 composer Akhmet Zhubanov published a detailed account in Kazakhstanskaya Pravda. In 1984, the inclusion of orteke in the Murager state cultural program helped rescue the practice from Soviet-era obscurity.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The kinetic dance of orteke is performed not by human bodies stepping across a floor, but by mechanical proxy through an articulated puppet operated by a seated musician. The instrumentalist, known as a küyshi, sits holding a two-stringed dombra. Strings or threads are fastened to the musician's playing fingers or wrists and run to the puppet, which is mounted on a metal rod over a dauylpaz drum or table. As the musician executes rhythmic strumming, finger-striking, and plucking on the instrument, the tension on the strings jerks the puppet's hinged legs. The puppet hops, kicks, and taps the surface in strict synchrony with the musical tempo. The movement intentionally mimics the frantic, agile jumping of a wild mountain goat trying to leap out of a pit. Advanced masters manipulate multiple figurines at once using both hands and feet, adding intricate percussive accents to the performance.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical foundation of orteke is provided by the dombra (or dombyra), the traditional two-stringed Kazakh long-necked plucked lute. The sound of the plucked strings is acoustically doubled by the percussive impact of the wooden goat striking the skin of a dauylpaz drum, functioning as an integrated self-accompanying percussion system. Virtuosic performers expand the musical palette by incorporating wind instruments such as the sazsyrnay (a traditional clay ocarina) or the shankobyz (jaw harp). The repertoire consists of instrumental küy compositions, historically composed and performed by renowned küyshis including Tattimbet, Bayserke, Shashubay, and Nawryzbay. Performances are entirely instrumental and devoid of spoken dialogue, focusing on the dynamic acoustic dialogue between lute strings and goat-hoof taps.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occur in intimate or theatrical indoor and outdoor gathering spaces. The physical apparatus rests upon a wooden table draped with traditional animal skin or fabric decorated with national Kazakh embroidery. The puppet, historically assembled from dried mountain goat skin stuffed with straw in the Semirechye region, is more universally carved from red birch, walnut, maple, ash, or oak wood. The animal features curved horns and flexible joints attached via strings to the performer's digits, mounted firmly above a drum surface via a metal rod. The küyshi typically wears traditional Kazakh dress suited for formal instrumental concerts and community festivals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally staged within nomadic encampments and domestic gatherings, orteke serves as an artistic tribute to wildlife, pastoral life, and the rugged mountain ecology inhabited by wild goats. Beyond its historical associations with shamanic healing, the performance functions as an entertaining and educational medium of communication between adults and children. In modern times, orteke is presented at community celebrations, national holiday concerts, the biennial Orteke International Festival, and regional puppetry competitions.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical figures linked to the master repertoire of orteke melodies include classical küyshis Tattimbet, Bayserke, Shashubay, and Nawryzbay. In 1935, Kazakh composer and academic Akhmet Kuanovich Zhubanov provided the first detailed modern analysis of the art form. In the contemporary revival, the musical ensembles Er-Turan and Hassak have brought orteke to international attention, while educators and researchers at the Kokil Musical College in Almaty have led academic documentation and training.
sections.regional_variants: Within Kazakhstan, construction methods vary regionally; the Semirechye region historically utilized real goat hide filled with straw, while western and central regions favoured carved timber from birch, walnut, ash, and oak. Across Central Asia, cognate traditions exist among neighbouring nomadic cultures. In Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and northern Afghanistan, an analogous goat-and-lute puppetry performance is known as buz-bazi. In Kyrgyzstan, the related tradition is termed takteke, which typically features two carved puppets engaged in a simulated combat upon a sounding box, accompanied by the three-stringed komuz.
sections.lineage: Orteke descends from ancient Turkic pastoral puppetry and shamanic performance traditions. During the twentieth century, it transitioned through Soviet folklore programs, including the 1984 Murager national registry. It belongs to the broader Central Asian nomadic family of mechanical puppetry traditions alongside Kyrgyz takteke and Afghan buz-bazi, with lineage preserved today through master-apprentice lineages, academic research at Almaty's Kokil Musical College, and festival competitions.

sections.origins_and_history: Rejang is an ancient sacred Balinese dance, conceived as a sacrificial offering in which girls present themselves before Hindu deities. Practiced across Hindu sanctuaries in Bali, the dance forms a core element of cyclic religious calendar rites designed to greet divine spirits descending to Earth.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance takes the form of a harmonious procession. Participants undergo no prior formal training, believing that the spirit of ngayah guides their bodies to move in complete unison. Girls as young as two or three years old join the communal line, moving together under shared devotion.

sections.occasions_and_meaning: The word 'Rejang' translates directly to 'offering'. It serves as a greeting ceremony for gods arriving on Earth during major milestones of the Balinese ceremonial calendar. The act embodies the concept of ngayah, or spiritual community service and devotion.

sections.origins_and_history: The Pyrrhichios originated in ancient Greece, likely of Dorian origin, with roots tracing back to Minoan Crete. Historical references identify figures like Thaletas of Crete as a musical arranger for these dances in Sparta. It was performed widely across the Greek world from the Black Sea to Cyprus, evolving from practical battle preparation into a staple of civic festivals, athletic games, and symposia.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers wore full hoplite armor, carrying shields, spears, and helmets. The choreography involved quick movements simulating the avoidance of blows and darts, attacking enemies, advancing, retreating, dropping to the ground as if wounded, and springing back up. It was performed as a solo, in dueling pairs facing each other, or in large circular groups by men, youths, boys, and occasionally women.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance was exclusively accompanied by the sound of the aulos, a double-reed ancient Greek wind instrument. The musical time was quick and light, corresponding directly to the metric foot known as the pyrrhic.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wore complete military armor including helmets, greaves, shields, and tunics—often traditionally associated with the vermilion red color of blood. Settings ranged from Spartan training grounds and the Athenian palaestra to festive banquets (symposia) and grand ritual spaces during the Panathenaic Games and Gymnopédies.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance was deeply tied to religious cults honoring Zeus, Cybèle, Artemis, Athena, and the Dioscuri. It served a dual purpose: practical martial training to increase warrior agility before battle, and ritual performance during funerals, civic games, and diplomatic banquets to celebrate unity or victory.
sections.notable_figures: Achilles is mythically credited by Aristotle with creating the dance around Patroclus's funeral pyre. Xenophon documented its performance at a banquet in Kotyora, and Plato detailed its tactical mechanics in his work Leges.
sections.regional_variants: Regional expressions varied from the strict martial training drills of Sparta to the competitive displays of Athenian youth in the Panathenaic Games. Ancient sources also note derivative or related forms such as the epikridios, orsitès, apikrènios, apokinos, and maktrismos.
sections.lineage: The dance shares a lineage with other ancient Greek armed dances and ritual traditions such as the dances of the Korybantes and Curetes, influencing later historical conceptions of European weapon dances.

sections.origins_and_history: Dance references in Jewish history date back to the Bible and Talmud, which contain over 30 distinct dance terms. During the dispersion, national community dancing ceased until the halutzim (pioneers) of the First, Second, and Third Aliyahs (1882–1923) reintroduced dances brought from the Diaspora, establishing the horah as the national dance. Choreographer Rivka Sturman created over 90 dances between 1942 and 1983 to provide children with indigenous cultural reflections. Gurit Kadman organized the first First Fruits pageant at kibbutz Dalia in 1944, establishing regular festivals. The Karmiel Dance Festival, launched in 1988, is now Israel's largest dance celebration.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dances feature fixed choreographies matched to specific musical pieces selected by a yotzer (choreographer). Formations include circles, couples, trios, short lines, and group line formations. Movement is highly varied, incorporating the Tza'ad Temani, Horah, and dabke. The pioneer horah was performed at a breakneck pace with dancers linking arms over each other's shoulders.
sections.music_and_instruments: Dances are usually performed to songs in Hebrew, traditional klezmer music, and other popular Israeli genres, archetypally represented by Hava Nagila.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dances are performed publicly in towns and cities, notably on beachfronts and promenades (tayelets), as well as at kibbutzim, festivals, and communal gatherings.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Created to help build a new Israeli culture and celebrate the pioneering spirit, dances are performed at life-cycle events like weddings and bar/bat mitzvahs, holiday celebrations such as Shavuot, and regular weekly recreational sessions.
sections.notable_figures: Rivka Sturman created over 90 classic Israeli dances between 1942 and 1983. Gurit Kadman organized the first Shavuot dance pageant and folk dance festival at kibbutz Dalia in 1944. Baruch Agadati introduced the horah to the Mandate of Palestine in 1924.
sections.regional_variants: Influences include the European Hora, Hasidic dance traditions, the Middle Eastern Arabic dabke, and Yemenite steps. Newer dances incorporate jazz and disco formats, such as Yo Ya and Zodiak.
sections.lineage: Rooted in Diaspora folk dances brought by pioneers (including the horah, polka, Krakowiak, Czerkassiya, and rondo) combined with Middle Eastern and Jewish religious dance traditions.

sections.origins_and_history: Ukusina originates from South Africa's coastal region among the Zulu people. The etymology stems from the verb sina ('to dance') and the prefix uku-. Passed down primarily through oral traditions, the dance has been actively preserved and promoted against modernization through cultural festivals and institutions.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance features tremendous dexterity and vigor, led by an induna who sets the pace. Movements include powerful leg kicks in any direction up and out, ground-stamping of each foot, hops, and deft hand movements performed in line or circular patterns.
sections.music_and_instruments: Performances are socially created around a song leader singing interlocking word phrases. The rhythmic foundation is provided by traditional Zulu drums and other percussion instruments.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear intricate beadwork on headdresses, necklaces, bracelets, and anklets, alongside animal-skin clothing from cows and goats and spiritual feathers. Men wear an ibheshu or isikhakha, while women wear an isidwaba.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Ukusina is performed at weddings, memorial services, and coming-of-age ceremonies. It serves as a spiritual ritual to communicate with ancestors and request blessings, alongside its role in social entertainment.
sections.notable_figures: The induna serves as the lead competent dancer who sets the pace and directs other participants.

claims.text: Bwola, also known as Acholi bwola, is a traditional dance that originates from the Acholi people in Northern Uganda.
It is reserved for special occasions and performances in front of royalty, including kings and chiefs.
The dancers move in a circular motion, with the men moving in a clockwise direction and the women moving in an anti-clockwise direction.
Bwola is recognized by its distinct elements such as calabash called "Larakaraka" and a cylindrical drum known as "Jagi".

Dancers adorn themselves in traditional attire, including an ostrich-feather headdress, a white cloth elegantly draped around their waist, and ankle bells that add a rhythmic touch to their movements.
The practice of Bwola has encountered challenges, including the prohibition of specific animal parts that are crucial to the dance, thus posing a threat to its cultural preservation.

sections.origins_and_history: Umxhentso originates from the Xhosa people of South Africa, with its roots deeply tied to the Transkei homeland in the Eastern Cape. It has historically served as a central component of Xhosa ceremonies and the work of traditional healers.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves barefoot stomping and vigorous upper-body movement. A key technique is ukutyityimba, which involves shaking the thoracic region and the upper body. It is often accompanied by rhythmic clapping.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music includes the Uhadi musical bow, drum beats, and the use of a whistle called an Impempe, made from Ingcongolo reed. Vocal accompaniment is provided through the composition and singing of theme songs called ukombela.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear beaded garments called umbhaco. Dancers often paint their bodies prior to performance. The dance is primarily performed in the Transkei homeland in the Eastern Cape.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Umxhentso is performed at weddings (Umdudo), initiation ceremonies for healers (Intlombe), rites of passage for boys (Umguyo), and ritual ceremonies for women (Umngqungqo).
sections.notable_figures: not described in sources
sections.regional_variants: The dance varies by context: Umngqungqo (women's ritual), Umdudo (weddings), Intlombe (healer initiation), and Umguyo (boys' initiation).

claims.text: Umxhentso is the traditional dancing of Xhosa people performed mostly by Amagqirha, the traditional healers/Sangoma.
The dance includes overt shoulder movements that include shaking the thoracic region, known as ukutyityimba, and stomping barefoot.
Umxhentso is usually accompanied by a drum beat or slow vocal music called ukombela with clapping to give the dancers a rhythm to follow.
Xhosa people wear beaded clothes called umbhaco when they perform umxhentso.
Umxhentso is mostly performed in the Transkei homeland in the Eastern Cape Province of South Africa where the tradition is still valued.
Intlombe is performed by traditional healers/Amagqira during their initiation ceremonies.

sections.origins_and_history: The Ayyalah originated as a Bedouin war dance performed after tribal victories. It historically served as a ritual for tribal unity when groups were threatened by enemies. In 2014, it was recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves two rows of men facing each other. Participants carry bamboo sticks, swords, or rifles. They move their heads and sticks synchronously with the drum rhythm while hopping from one foot to another. Women participate in the naash ritual, tossing their hair.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features large and small drums, tambourines, brass cymbals, leather bagpipes, and flutes. The melody consists of seven tones in an irregular repeated pattern.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men wear the traditional white dishdasha. Women wear traditional dresses. The dance is performed in open spaces during weddings, national celebrations, and official state visits.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed for weddings, national holidays, state visits, and football matches. It signifies tribal solidarity, victory, and the protection of the community.
sections.notable_figures: The lead performer is typically an inherited role responsible for training other dancers.

claims.text: The yowlah, or Al Ayyala dance, involves dance, drum music, and chanted poetry; its routine is meant to simulate a battle scene.
Two rows of about twenty men face each other, carrying thin sticks of bamboo to signify spears or swords.
The yowlah is recorded (as al-ayyala) on UNESCO's Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage Items of Humanity in November 2014.
The yowlah originated as a Bedouin war dance where men would spin rifles after victory in a battle.
In the United Arab Emirates, girls wearing traditional dresses stand at the front, tossing their long hair from side to side.
In Oman the dancers arrange themselves in two rows facing each other and moving forward, swaying back and forth to simulate the head of a moving camel.

sections.origins_and_history: Originating with the Ndau people of Zimbabwe, the dance historically served as a preparation and celebration for warriors. It has evolved into a presentational dance for community gatherings and cultural festivals.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced in a cow horn formation, the performance involves synchronized foot-stomping, rhythmic clapping, and whistling. It progresses from a solo introduction (Mungeneso) to group choreography (chibhubhubhu) and individual displays (chigiyo).
sections.music_and_instruments: The music relies on rhythmic drumming and vocal singing. Women provide the vocal accompaniment and rhythmic clapping to support the male dancers.

sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed at weddings, chief installations, harvest festivals, and burials of royals. It is a secular dance used for entertainment and cultural celebration.

claims.text: Muchongoyo is a presentational dance and drumming style that emphasizes acrobatic and stomping sequences to dazzle spectators during gatherings or competitions with a complementary rythme of sharp claps.
The word Muchongoyo comes from the Ndau word kuchongoya, which means to stamp one's foot.
The purpose of the violent foot stomping in muchongoyo is historically to chastise warriors before battle and to celebrate success afterward.
A lead guy known as chikopo performs a solo introductory act known as Mungeneso to introduce the dance.

The dancers perform while wearing traditional attire, which for men includes mbikiza and vests on the body, either ngututu or feathers on the head, zvihlabvu or machoba on the legs and arms, and manyatera (sandals) on the feet.
Muchongolo is the name of it in Tsonga.
Muchongoyo is a traditional dance that is performed for celebratory purposes or events of cultural significance such as burials of chief and royals.

sections.origins_and_history: Ekikibi originated among the Bakonzo, a Bantu ethnic community inhabiting the Rwenzori mountain range spanning western Uganda and eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, predominantly across Kasese, Bundibugyo, Bunyangabu, and Ntoroko districts. The dance was conceived through the close observation and admiration of fish swimming in mountain streams, translating aquatic locomotion into human choreography. Influenced over centuries by the alpine environment and cultural practices of the Rwenzori heights, Ekikibi has been transmitted across generations as an emblem of Bakonzo identity.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by an ensemble usually consisting of four men and four women arrayed in concentric circles, with the men charting an outer path and women holding the inner ring. Performers execute rhythmic steps, vertical jumps, twists, and complete turns designed to mimic the agile motion of fish in water. As the concentric formations rotate, the dancers continuously exchange focused eye contact and expressive hand gestures to convey emotional intimacy, affection, and mutual joy.
sections.music_and_instruments: Ekikibi is accompanied by vocal love songs specifically composed to praise the character and union of the bride and groom. The instrumental backing is anchored by drums providing percussive cadence, supplemented by rattles for sharp rhythmic texture and flutes carrying melodic phrases. The interplay of instruments supports the undulating tempo required for the dancers' twists, turns, and jumps.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance is performed in festive outdoor village clearings, ceremonial reception spaces, or wedding venues across the Rwenzori foothills. Performers wear vibrant, colorful traditional costumes accompanied by decorative adornments that highlight the visual flair of rapid turns and aquatic mimicry.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Staged principally during weddings and communal festive gatherings, Ekikibi celebrates love, marriage, and domestic happiness. It articulates harmony and mutual respect between bride and groom as well as their respective families. In addition to social celebration, the dance honors ancestors and deities, invoking their blessings and spiritual protection over the newly forged marital union.

sections.origins_and_history: The ballet-féerie originated in Russia as a synthesis of the French féerie theatrical genre and the Italian ballo grande dance style. It evolved from a long history of European spectacle, including the Renaissance ballet de cour and 17th-century pièces à machines, which relied on the engineering of architects like Nicola Sabbatini. In the 19th century, these influences merged with the Russian interest in narrative ballet, creating a genre that prioritized visual transformation and ensemble performance.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Technique not described in sources. The genre is noted for prioritizing ensemble dances and shifting stage pictures over individual solo virtuosity.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music of the ballet-féerie is characterized by its symphonic scale and ability to support narrative transformations. Tchaikovsky’s works are the primary examples, utilizing full orchestral arrangements to underscore the magical and supernatural elements of the plot.
sections.costume_and_setting: Settings were defined by lavish, mechanically worked stage effects including trapdoors, smoke machines, and quickly changeable sets. Costumes were designed to be brilliant and dazzling, often representing supernatural creatures like gnomes, witches, and fairies to heighten the moral tone of the production.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The ballet-féerie served as a popular, often commercialized form of entertainment that aimed to provide a 'dreamlike' experience for the audience. It functioned as a morality play, depicting the triumph of good over evil through the use of magic talismans and supernatural intervention.
sections.notable_figures: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky is the most significant figure associated with the genre, having composed The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker within this framework.
sections.regional_variants: The genre originated in France as a theatrical 'fairy play' (féerie) before being adapted into the Russian 'ballet-féerie.' Other variants include the English 'fairy extravaganza' and the Spanish 'comedia de magia.'
sections.lineage: The genre descends from the French féerie and the Italian ballo grande, serving as a precursor to modern spectacular stage productions.

sections.origins_and_history: Orunyege-Ntogoro originated in the pre-colonial era within the Bunyoro-Kitara and Tooro kingdoms of western Uganda. Historically, young people gathered under the moonlight to socialize, celebrate communal identity, and express romantic affection. The dance is an intentional synthesis of two distinct traditions: Orunyege, an acrobatic and energetic dance originating in Hoima and Fort Portal districts, and Ntogoro, a graceful, elegant style hailing from Masindi district. According to oral tradition, community elders organized public dance competitions when multiple suitors sought the hand of the same bride. The contest tested physical stamina and resilience, eliminating the first man to tire under the premise that an enduring dancer was best equipped to sustain a household through droughts or famine.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance is carried out by two distinct groups: male dancers known as abakwongezi and female dancers known as abakwetegerezi. The ensemble shifts dynamically across circular, linear, and paired formations under the direction of a master of ceremonies (omukama) and musical cues from the lead drummers. Dancers execute synchronized sequences punctuated by individual demonstrations of virtuosity, including high leaps, rapid spinning, and full-body shaking. Male dancers maintain sharp, percussive leg work that sounds their dried gourd leg rattles in strict alignment with drum rhythms. Female dancers execute smooth, coordinated footwork while using bead or cowrie-shell waist rings to accentuate isolated hip movements, balancing vigorous athleticism with elegant poise.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical foundation of Orunyege-Ntogoro relies on a live ensemble of drums, flutes, and xylophones. The drummers drive the performance, altering tempo, intensity, and rhythmic phrasing to steer the dancers through varying phases of endurance. Flutists and xylophonists weave melodic phrases and harmonies over the drum lines. The music is augmented acoustically by the dancers themselves: the ebinyege leg rattles worn by male dancers produce crisp rhythmic accompaniment with every footfall. The entire sonic environment is directed by the omukama, a master of ceremonies who leads the ensemble with sung chants, praise poetry, and humorous spoken banter.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes are designed to serve both acoustic and visual functions. Male dancers wear shirts and shorts, leaving the lower legs free to securely fasten ebinyege, which are rattles fashioned from dried gourds or calabashes. Female dancers wear long skirts and blouses, accented around the hips by entogoro—ornamental rings crafted from beads or cowrie shells that magnify the sway and rotation of the pelvis. Historically danced outdoors on bare earth in evening moonlight, the tradition is now commonly staged in school halls, cultural festivals, tourism venues, and ceremonial grounds.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally functioning as a primary courtship ritual, Orunyege-Ntogoro allowed young adults of the Bunyoro and Tooro communities to evaluate prospective partners on the basis of physical endurance, agility, and grace. It continues to be an integral part of traditional weddings, initiation rites, and Empaako naming ceremonies, as well as seasonal community celebrations. Ethnomusicologist Linda Cimardi notes that runyege serves as a vital medium for staging local culture, reinforcing traditional gender norms while also offering performers a space to negotiate personal expression.
sections.notable_figures: Ethnomusicologist Linda Cimardi has documented runyege as a wide performance genre encompassing singing, instrumentation, dance, and acting in western Uganda.
sections.regional_variants: The dance unites two distinct regional styles of western Uganda: the Orunyege component, which developed in the Hoima and Fort Portal districts and is known for its intense, athletic, and acrobatic character; and the Ntogoro component, which emerged from Masindi district and is defined by graceful, elegant movements.
sections.lineage: Orunyege-Ntogoro belongs to the runyege performance genre of the Banyoro and Batooro peoples, rooted in the heritage of the Bunyoro-Kitara and Tooro kingdoms.

claims.text: Orunyege-Ntogoro is a courtship dance of the Batooro and Banyoro communities of western Uganda.
The name Entogoro derives from ebinyege, which are pod rattles tied to dancers' legs.
The dance unites Orunyege from Hoima and Fort Portal with Ntogoro from Masindi.
Orunyege is characterized as energetic and acrobatic, whereas Ntogoro is graceful and elegant.
Male dancers are called abakwongezi and female dancers are called abakwetegerezi.
Female dancers wear rings made of beads or cowrie shells on their waists called entogoro.
The performance is accompanied by an ensemble of drums, flutes, and xylophones.
A master of ceremonies known as omukama leads the performance with praises and jokes.
Oral tradition states suitors competed in dancing where the first man to tire was eliminated.
The dance continues to be actively practiced in cultural festivals and ceremonies today.

sections.origins_and_history: Orunyege-Ntogoro dates to the pre-colonial era of the Bunyoro-Kitara and Tooro kingdoms in western Uganda, where it served as both a social gathering and an athletic courtship contest. Young people convened during evening social gatherings to dance under moonlight. Oral traditions recount that when several suitors sought the hand of the same bride, community elders organized an open dance competition. The first suitor to collapse from fatigue was eliminated, while the victor demonstrated the stamina and resilience deemed essential for protecting and sustaining a household during times of drought or famine.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by two ensembles: male dancers (abakwongezi) and female dancers (abakwetegerezi). Dancers assemble in circles, lines, and paired arrangements, responding to musical cues from the drummers and the omukama (master of ceremonies). Men execute energetic foot stomps, spins, and jumps that activate their leg rattles, while women perform graceful hip movements that oscillate their beaded waist rings. Both groups demonstrate synchronized ensemble footwork interspersed with solo improvisations that highlight stamina, balance, and agility.
sections.music_and_instruments: Musical accompaniment is provided by an ensemble of drums, traditional flutes, and xylophones. The drummers dictate transitions, shifting rhythmic density and tempo in response to the dance's dramatic arc. Flutes and xylophones overlay interlocking melodic contours and harmonies. The performance is directed by a master of ceremonies (omukama), who leads vocal chants, sings praise poetry, and delivers humorous commentary to engage the audience.
sections.costume_and_setting: Male dancers wear shirts and shorts, with ebinyege—rattles fashioned from dried gourds or calabashes—fastened securely to their legs. Female dancers wear long skirts and blouses, girded at the waist with entogoro rings made of cowrie shells or beads designed to accentuate hip articulations. Traditionally performed outdoors on bare earth under moonlight, contemporary performances take place at cultural festivals, wedding receptions, tourism exhibitions, and school auditoriums.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Entogoro functions as a courtship showcase, community celebration, and instructional medium for transmitting social etiquette. It is traditionally performed during weddings, youth initiation ceremonies, social gatherings, and Empaako naming rituals. The dance serves as an educational vehicle, instructing younger generations on community standards regarding courtship, resilience, and mutual respect between partners.
sections.notable_figures: The master of ceremonies, designated as the omukama, serves as the central artistic director of the performance, steering the musicians and dancers through vocal calls. Ethnomusicologist Linda Cimardi has documented and analyzed the wider runyege performance genre in western Uganda, examining its role in cultural preservation and gender dynamics.
sections.regional_variants: The dance synthesizes two regional forms: Orunyege, hailing from the Hoima and Fort Portal districts, which features highly energetic and acrobatic movements; and Ntogoro, originating from the Masindi district, which emphasizes graceful, fluid, and elegant posturing.
sections.lineage: Originating within the ancestral courts and rural settlements of the Bunyoro-Kitara and Tooro kingdoms, the dance is sustained by the Batooro and Banyoro communities. It is passed down through family apprenticeship, community ceremonies, and formal instruction in Ugandan schools and cultural performance troupes.

basic_steps: Stomp the right foot into the floor to sound the leg rattle (ebinyege) on the downbeat.
Transfer weight smoothly to the left foot while engaging a quick rebound strike.
Isolate and circle the hips rhythmically so the waist ring (entogoro) swings laterally.
Execute an explosive vertical hop, landing simultaneously on both feet to produce a unified rattle crash.
Perform a controlled spin on the ball of the foot while sustaining continuous hip rotation.
teaching.rhythm: Polyrhythmic drumming patterns alternating between steady driving tempos and accelerating cadence cues.
teaching.formation: Concentric or open circles, parallel facing lines of men and women, and individual courtship pairings.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners must master ankle stability and rattle timing before attempting continuous spins or vertical leaps.

claims.text: Entogoro is a traditional courtship dance of the Batooro and Banyoro communities of western Uganda.
The dance combines traditions from different districts, with Orunyege originating in Hoima and Fort Portal, and Ntogoro hailing from Masindi.
Orunyege is characterized by acrobatic energy, whereas Ntogoro is recognized for its grace and elegance.
Male dancers wear ebinyege rattles made of dried calabashes or gourds tied to their legs.
Female dancers wear entogoro rings crafted from beads or cowrie shells around their waists to accentuate hip movements.
The performance is accompanied by an ensemble of drums, flutes, and xylophones, directed by a master of ceremonies.
Oral traditions describe a courtship contest where multiple suitors danced to exhaustion so elders could select the most resilient husband.
The dance continues to be actively practiced today across western Uganda in festivals, schools, and cultural ceremonies.

sections.origins_and_history: Naleyo is rooted among the Karamajong people, an agro-pastoral ethnic group living in North Eastern Uganda who speak the Nilotic language NgaKarimojong. The dance functions as an annual post-harvest custom, emerging from seasonal rhythms to provide a structured gathering for celebration and social bonding.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in two parallel lines with women in one line and men arranged in the opposite line facing one another. Dancers face each other across the divide and execute energetic, high vertical jumps. In this setting, women actively choose their male dancing partners as the two lines interact.
sections.music_and_instruments: Accompaniment is provided by traditional instruments, specifically the adungu (arched harp), the ngoma (drum), and the ekitirikiti (shakers or percussive instruments). These instruments supply the melodic and rhythmic backdrop that drives the dancers' repeated vertical leaps.
sections.costume_and_setting: Men wear traditional attire including a headdress made of animal skin, an animal hide skirt, and a beaded belt. Women dress in an animal hide skirt and beaded necklaces. The dance is held outdoors during the post-harvest period in North Eastern Uganda.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Naleyo is held annually after the harvest season as a wooing and courtship celebration. It provides a recognized cultural venue for young men and women to find love and select suitors, while serving as a broader expression of Karamajong cultural heritage.

basic_steps: Form two opposing, parallel lines with men in one line and women in the other, directly facing across the floor.
Engage the core and bend both knees to prepare an explosive vertical rebound.
Jump straight up off both feet, driving vertically into the air while keeping the torso upright and maintaining eye contact with the opposite line.
Land softly on the balls of both feet with knees flexed, keeping the rhythm steady.
Women step forward from their line to designate and dance facing their chosen partner.

claims.text: Ekitaguriro is a traditional dance originating from the Ankole region in southwestern Uganda.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance is rooted in the Natha Pantha tradition and is performed by the Arebhahse people of Sullia. It is a traditional, religious folk dance that has been passed down through generations.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers gather at a holy place, then move from house to house. They set up a lamp in the courtyard and dance around it. The performance involves mythological mimicry, acting, singing, and dancing. The Sanyasi character roams the courtyard independently while the others perform.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music consists of singing and rhythmic chanting. Instruments mentioned include the conch and the drum, which are carried by the Dasayya character.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes vary by character: the Sanyasi wears dried camouflage leaves and a symbolic wooden phallus; the Bhatru wears a white dhoti, sacred thread, and sandalwood paste; the Dasayya wears a white dhoti, red shawl, and carries a conch and drum; the Koraga uses dark body paint; the Byari wears a white banyan and a traditional hat.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed during the full moon of the Suggi month. It is a religious and traditional folk dance that involves visiting homes to perform for the community.

sections.origins_and_history: The tradition originated in the 14th or 15th century in the Iwate Prefecture, rooted in the worship of Mount Hayachine. It was historically performed by shrine officers and is believed to have been influenced by the practices of yamabushi, mountain-dwelling Buddhist ascetics. Scholars continue to investigate its potential links to the history of Noh theater.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The performance consists of twelve dances, with dancers wearing masks. The final dance features a performer as a shishi, a lion-like creature. The full cycle lasts five hours. Specific footwork and gesture techniques are not described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is performed by an ensemble using drums, cymbals, and flutes. This musical accompaniment supports the twelve ritual dances.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear masks during the dances. The primary setting is the Hayachine Shrine in Hanamaki, Iwate, where the performance takes place on August 1st, though it is also performed in other locations.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dances are performed in honor of Seoritsu, the tutelary deity of Mount Hayachine. The performance serves to demonstrate the power of the mountain deity, bless the people, and reconfirm the identity of the community.
sections.notable_figures: not described in sources
sections.regional_variants: While the main tradition is at Hayachine Shrine, 'discipleship' shows are performed throughout the Iwate Prefecture, though rarely as the full twelve-dance cycle.
sections.lineage: The tradition is a type of Kagura, a category of ritual dance in Shinto ceremonies.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in the African American community of the Carolinas in the 1920s. It was initially a street dance before being standardized by the Arthur Murray studios in the late 1930s. The name 'collegiate' was applied to distinguish it from other regional shag variations popular among the youth of the era.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced in a closed, offset position. The basic step is a six-count pattern: slow (step-hop), slow (step-hop), quick (step), quick (step). Dancers maintain a constant vertical pulse on the balls of their feet. Arms are often held high, with the lead's right hand on the follow's back and the follow's left arm on the lead's shoulder.
sections.music_and_instruments: Performed to uptempo swing and pre-swing jazz music, including Dixieland and Gypsy-Jazz. The tempo is typically between 185 and 250+ beats per minute.
sections.costume_and_setting: Historically associated with 1930s collegiate social settings. Modern practice occurs in dance studios, festivals, and social dance events.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a social dance for youth in the 1930s and 40s. Today, it is practiced at swing dance festivals and social dance nights worldwide.
sections.notable_figures: Ryan Martin, who released the 2014 film 'The Rebirth of Shag'.
sections.regional_variants: Carolina Shag and St. Louis Shag are distinct dances that share the name but are not directly related to Collegiate Shag.
sections.lineage: Part of the swing family of American vernacular dances; shares roots with other 1920s African American dances.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated among enslaved African descendants in Maranhão. The earliest known record dates to 1818, described as a 'batuque.' It was officially registered as Brazilian Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2007.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in a circle. Women (coreiras) dance individually in the center, inviting others via the 'punga' (a belly-to-belly bump). Men (coureiros) play drums and lead the singing.
sections.music_and_instruments: The ensemble consists of three drums (parelhas): the crivador (small), meião (medium), and roncador (large). Additional instruments include the pandeiro and matracas.
sections.costume_and_setting: Women wear wide, colorful skirts, lace blouses, and turbans with floral adornments. Men wear white pants, straw hats, and patterned shirts. It is performed in squares, terreiros, or at social events.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: It is performed for Saint Benedict, birthdays, social gatherings, and celebrations like Carnival or June festivals.

The punga or umbigada is a peculiar choreography marked by a belly-to-belly movement.

Historical records of the dance date back to 1818.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated during the Edo period, influenced by the dances of visiting sailors. By the middle of the eighteenth century, it had become a performance showcase for local girls. In 1976, the Japanese government designated it as an intangible cultural heritage, and in 2009, it was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, later being incorporated into the Furyu-odori category in 2022.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Ten to twenty girls, aged 5 to 12, perform in two rows facing each other or in a circle. They hold bamboo strips in their hands and strike them together to create a rhythmic sound. The dancers are accompanied by an a cappella choir of older women.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is provided entirely by an a cappella choir of five to ten older women. The only instrumental element is the rhythmic clicking of bamboo strips held by the dancers, which produces the signature sound of the performance.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dancers wear colorful kimono. The performance takes place on January 15th at local shrines or in front of houses within the community in Miura, Japan.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance is performed to celebrate the New Year and to invoke good fortune, specifically targeting prosperity and abundant fishing catches for the community.

claims.text: Chakkirako is a dance performed at a festival in Miura, Japan, to celebrate the New Year and bring good fortune, especially in fishing.
In 2009, it was inscribed in UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and in 2022, it was incorporated into the broader subject of Furyu-odori.
The dance originated in the Edo period with influences by the dances of visiting sailors.
Every year in the middle of January, ten to twenty girls in colorful kimono between the ages of 5 and 12 perform the dance at a shrine or in front of houses.
They are accompanied by five to ten older women singing a capella.
The dancers hold bamboo strips in their hands and strike them together, which produces the sound that gives the dance its name.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in the 16th century under Ratu Melinting II. It was originally called Cetik Kipas and was exclusively performed by the royal family. In 1965, President Sukarno renamed it Melinting and introduced it to a national audience at Istora Senayan.

claims.text: Melinting is one of the traditional dances from Lampung province, Indonesia.
It was originally known as the Cetik Kipas dance before its name was changed to Melinting dance.
The name change was proposed by President Sukarno, who asked the Central Lampung Regional Government to perform the dance at Istora Senayan Jakarta on August 17, 1965.
Melinting is a dance inherited from Ratu Melinting, which is estimated to have existed in the sixteenth century.
The movements in dancing are divided into two categories based on gender, with a total of eight dancers: four men and four women.
The Melinting dance costume for men consists of tapis cloth, a belanga shirt, seretei feathers (Bulu seretei), a fan with free colors, and a gold Skullcap.
